name: Poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA)

lead: PDLLA is a dissolvable polymer injected into skin to trigger the body to make new collagen, rather than just to plump a spot. It is used for wrinkles, nasolabial folds, scars and skin quality, and sits alongside PLLA and calcium hydroxylapatite in the biostimulator category.
Published support consists of a few randomised and open-label trials plus reviews; forum discussion appears to be minimal.

paras: As the particles break down into lactic acid, the body mounts a mild inflammatory response and fibroblasts lay down collagen over weeks to months.

Reviews highlight granuloma formation and non-inflammatory nodules, which may need treatment such as triamcinolone. As with other fillers, the FDA notes some complications appear long after injection and that rare vascular events can occur.

lead: Poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) is a biodegradable synthetic polymer used in injectable skin products classed as biostimulators. Rather than simply filling a space, biostimulatory fillers such as PDLLA, poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), polycaprolactone and calcium hydroxylapatite are described as prompting a controlled inflammatory response that leads the body to produce new collagen [1][2][3].

Reviews describe PDLLA as improving skin elasticity and firmness, reducing wrinkles and supporting tissue regeneration and scar remodelling, while noting that granuloma formation and non-inflammatory nodules are recognised complications [1]. One commercial product, AestheFill (REGEN Biotech, South Korea), has been compared with hyaluronic acid in a randomised nasolabial fold trial [4]. PDLLA is also used in non-cosmetic settings such as bone fixation screws and drug-delivery particles, which are separate from the injectable use [1][5].
The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of PDLLA, and the published cosmetic evidence is a small set of trials and reviews.

paras: PLA exists in two stereoisomeric forms, PLLA and PDLLA, which can differ in handling and clinical performance [2]. As PLA particles degrade into lactic acid, they stimulate fibroblasts to synthesise collagen, and the foreign-body response leads to fibrous tissue formation [2]. A 2026 review of cytokine mechanisms proposes that PLLA, PDLLA, polycaprolactone and calcium hydroxylapatite all promote new collagen formation through regulated inflammatory and cytokine cascades [3]. Another 2026 review cautions that the word "regenerative" is used in aesthetic medicine without much biological precision and that it overlaps with repair, remodelling and biostimulation [6].

Cosmetic uses studied include nasolabial folds, photoaged skin, acne scars and gluteal skin laxity [4][7][8][9]. Outside appearance medicine, PDLLA appears in resorbable bone screws and in bone augmentation devices, and as micro- and nanoparticles for drug delivery [1][5].

Granuloma formation and non-inflammatory nodules are the complications highlighted in reviews, which stress monitoring and early intervention [1]. A 2024 case report describes a granuloma after PDLLA injection treated with triamcinolone [10]. The US FDA's general information on dermal fillers lists nodules or granulomas as less common and permanent hard nodules and vascular injury as rare, and notes that some effects can appear long after injection.

A randomised, evaluator-blinded, multicentre trial compared AestheFill PDLLA with hyaluronic acid for nasolabial fold augmentation; its authors noted that efficacy and safety had not previously been studied in a large cohort [4]. A 2026 multicentre split-face randomised trial compared a PDLLA-based product with PLLA on the nasolabial fold [11]. An open-label prospective trial examined PDLLA injected with microneedle fractional radiofrequency for acne scars [8].

Registered studies include a split-face randomised study of PDLLA for photoaged skin pigmentation (40 participants) and a small study of PDLLA with ultrasound and radiofrequency for buttock fat and laxity (10 participants) [7][9]. Outcomes for these registrations are not given in the sources used here.
